Sample text:
---
On the first Monday of every month, my father took the forks out of the kitchen drawer and counted them. There were supposed to be twelve. If there were eleven, he went looking: under the sofa, behind the radiator, in the patch of yard where my sister and I had once tried to grow a fork tree. If there were thirteen, he looked genuinely troubled. A missing fork could be found. An extra fork meant somebody else, somewhere, was looking.

I thought this was how adults spent their Mondays. It was a surprise to marry a man who had no idea how many forks he owned.

“Enough,” he said.

“For what?”

He looked at the two plates on the table. “For tonight.”

We had been married nine years when my father moved in with us. He brought two suitcases, a radio, and a pillowcase tied at the neck with orange string. Inside were his forks. Eleven.

“One to go,” he said.

By then his fingers had stiffened. He could still count the forks, but he couldn't always separate them. My son Leo helped, lining them up on a dish towel. When they were finished, my father told him about the fork tree. I was doing the washing-up. I heard the exact moment my son began to believe in it: his chair scraped back.

“Where did you plant it?”

“Beside the garage.”

“Did you water it?”

“For a while. Then your mother got interested in roller skates.”

This was unfair. I had watered that fork well into November.

Leo considered the matter for several days. On Saturday he asked if we might go to the old house and dig it up. I explained that the house belonged to another family now. You couldn't just go into somebody's garden with a shovel.

“You could ask,” he said.

Which was true, though much of adulthood, in my experience, consisted of arranging your life so you didn't have to.

I wrote a note. A woman named Janet called me. She had been meaning to take out the bed beside the garage anyway. Sunday would be fine. Did we want to stay for tea?

My father wore a tie. Leo took a spoon for digging, on the theory that the shovel might damage the roots. My husband came along because, he said, there was no possible way he was missing this.

The garage was smaller than I remembered. Janet lent us a kneeling pad and showed us where a gas pipe ran. We found a green marble, a roofing nail, and the little white wheel from a toy ambulance. After half an hour Leo sat back on his heels, streaked with mud.

“Maybe somebody picked it,” he said.

My father was sitting on an upturned bucket. He had done very little digging. Now he put one hand into the pocket of his good coat and took out a fork.

For a second I was furious. Leo had dug a hole. Janet had made sandwiches. I had spent the morning in a state of tenderness toward my father that was difficult enough to sustain without his producing the whole point of the expedition from his pocket.

Then I saw that his hand was shaking. He wasn't sure how to get the fork into the hole without being seen. He had undertaken, at eighty-three, to perform a piece of magic for the first time in his life, and he hadn't thought to rehearse.

My husband tipped over the bucket.

It was an excellent diversion. There was a shout; my father caught my husband's sleeve; Janet rescued the plate of sandwiches. When order was restored, a silver tine poked out of the soil beside Leo's shoe.

Leo drew the fork out slowly. He wiped it on his trousers. He looked at my father.

“It's one of yours,” he said.

My father nodded.

“You brought it.”

“Yes.”

Leo turned the fork over. “Then you've only got ten at home.”

“That's right.”

“The next time you do a trick,” Leo said, “use one of Dad's. He doesn't count.”

We had tea against the warm wall of the garage. Janet kept the marble. Leo kept the ambulance wheel. Nobody wanted the nail.

Years later, when my father was gone and Leo was packing for his first flat, I found him in the kitchen with the pillowcase open on the table. He had taken out two forks.

“Is that enough?” I asked.

“For tonight,” he said, sounding so exactly like his father that I had to turn around and busy myself with the kettle.

After he left, I put the remaining forks away. They went in with the everyday ones, the bent one we used to fish toast out of the grill, the short one that had arrived with a takeaway salad and somehow survived three changes of address. I shut the drawer.

I don't count them. I do sometimes open the drawer on a Monday and move them about with my hand. They make a sound much like a person coming in with keys, someone familiar who doesn't need you to get up.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION. A tightly shaped family story uses the fork tree as a small magical premise for a tender, dryly comic account of inheritance and loss.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and wry, attentive to how affection often arrives disguised as fuss, mischief, or an ordinary household ritual. The narrator’s irritation at her father’s staged discovery gives way to recognition of his trembling hand and the care behind the trick. The ending invites the reader to feel grief as a familiar presence in daily life—not grand or resolved, but close enough to make the drawer sound like someone coming home.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds forks, counting, and the kitchen drawer as objects that carry family memory; a child’s willingness to believe; and the awkward, loving effort to make a small piece of magic. Its moral emphasis is gentle: tenderness may require accepting another person’s imperfect performance, and family habits can outlast the people who began them.

## Evidence line
> I do sometimes open the drawer on a Monday and move them about with my hand.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The story’s distinctive blend of domestic detail, dry humor, and restrained tenderness is sustained from the fork-counting ritual through the final image.
